name: Diminishing memory and the loss of personal identity in the afterlife
plain_explanation: Plotinus held that, contrary to what most people (including most modern theologians) would expect, the more the soul advances toward its true, eternal life after death, the less it remembers of its earthly relationships and personal history -- friends, family, one's very sense of individual personality gradually fade as the soul merges more fully with pure intellectual contemplation.
precise_definition: Plotinus's doctrine, in the Fourth Ennead (IV.4.2), that memory belongs strictly to the soul's temporal life, so that as the soul progresses toward eternal life it will remember progressively less of temporal particulars (spouse, children, personal identity), while nonetheless remaining, paradoxically, both distinct from and unified with nous ('simultaneously two and one').
why_it_mattered: Illustrates, for Russell, both Plotinus's logical consistency (following his premises about eternity and memory to their perhaps counter-intuitive conclusion) and the way his system subordinates ordinary human attachments to impersonal intellectual contemplation.
historical_origin: Developed in the Fourth Ennead's discussion of the soul.
examples: Plotinus's claim that sin is punished naturally through reincarnation, e.g. one who murders his mother will, in a future life, become a woman murdered by her own son
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Bears on Plotinus's doctrine of moral retribution through reincarnation.
